title: DfE Decoded #161: The Pay Rise Is the Headline. The Workload Changes May Matter More.
author: Paul Urry
source: paulurry68.substack.com (DfE Decoded, A Headteacher's Perspective), October 18, 2026
summary: Paul Urry works through England's new 2026 School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document and argues that the quieter workload and conditions changes matter more to school leaders than the salary tables. Pay rises 3.5 percent from September 2026 and a further 3 percent in 2027, but he focuses on the INSET flexibility that lets five days be delivered as the equivalent, for example as twilight sessions. He highlights a new Annex 6 list of 23 administrative tasks teachers should not routinely do, with a three-question test for whether a task needs a teacher at all. He also covers part-time TLR payments tied to the responsibility actually carried, a new non-consolidated recognition payment, clearer limits on weekend work and leader availability, off-site PPA by agreement, and a firmer line on rare cover. His leadership takeaway is that governors should discuss time, workload and flexibility with the same seriousness as the pay budget.
points: The document's three-question test (does the task need doing, is it administrative or clerical, does it require a teacher's judgement) gives schools a ready-made workload audit.
INSET can now be organised as the equivalent of five days, so twilight sessions or half-days can replace a single September training day if time is not simply added on top.
Part-time TLR payments must reflect the proportion of responsibility actually undertaken, which opens leadership roles to staff with different working patterns.
New wording protects leaders from permanent availability by limiting weekend work to genuine emergencies and promoting uninterrupted holiday time.
Urry's advice is that governors should discuss INSET, admin tasks, TLRs, recognition awards and cover alongside the pay tables, because those choices shape teachers' working lives.
quotes: But I don’t think the pay tables are the most interesting part of this year’s document.
Further in, some changes affect how we think about workload, INSET, TLRs, leadership time, recognition payments and some of the everyday tasks teachers have quietly ended up doing.
Sometimes, five carefully sequenced twilight sessions across a year might have more impact than one training day in September that everybody has forgotten by Christmas.
If the first two answers are yes and the third is no, it should not routinely be done by a teacher. That’s a pretty useful workload audit for any school.
Because many of these jobs didn’t arrive because somebody made a deliberate decision that teachers should do them. They just accumulated.
You’re paying for the responsibility. Not simply multiplying an allowance by somebody’s teaching fraction.
The fact that leadership isn’t governed by directed hours has sometimes become interpreted as: “You’re a leader, so you’re always working.” This document pushes back against that.
The salary tables tell us what teachers should be paid. Some of the quieter changes tell us rather more about how their time should be treated.
